options.A: 'Currency' is confined strictly to physical banknotes and coins, expressly excluding cheques, drafts, letters of credit, and credit cards from its definition
options.B: 'Currency Notes' means any negotiable instrument whatsoever, including cheques and bills of exchange, making it broader than - rather than a subset of - the definition of 'Currency'
options.C: 'Currency' and 'Currency Notes' are defined identically under FEMA, with no distinction drawn between the two terms in sections 2(h) and 2(i)

answer_html:

options.A: 'Foreign Exchange' is confined strictly to physical foreign currency notes and coins, expressly excluding deposits, credits, balances, drafts, travellers' cheques, letters of credit, or bills of exchange of any kind
options.B: 'Foreign Exchange' includes only instruments drawn and payable entirely in foreign currency, expressly excluding any instrument drawn in Indian currency but payable in foreign currency, or vice versa
options.C: 'Foreign Exchange' under FEMA is defined identically to 'Foreign Security', with the two terms used interchangeably throughout the Act

answer_html:

question_html: How does section 2(o) of FEMA, 1999 define 'Foreign Security', and what happens to a security's classification where it is denominated/expressed in foreign currency but redemption or return (such as interest or dividends) is payable in Indian currency?

options.A: 'Foreign Security' means any security, in the form of shares, stocks, bonds, debentures or any other instrument, denominated or expressed in foreign currency, and includes securities expressed in foreign currency but where redemption or any form of return such as interest or dividends is payable in Indian currency - such a security STILL qualifies as a 'Foreign Security' under this inclusive limb, despite the Indian-currency payability of its return
options.B: A security denominated in foreign currency automatically ceases to be a 'Foreign Security' the moment its redemption or return becomes payable in Indian currency, regardless of the inclusive language of section 2(o)
options.C: 'Foreign Security' is confined strictly to shares and stocks, expressly excluding bonds, debentures, or any other instrument denominated in foreign currency
options.D: 'Foreign Security' means any security issued by the Government of India, to the exclusion of any instrument issued by a private company or foreign entity

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) 'Foreign Security' means any security, in the form of shares, stocks, bonds, debentures or any other instrument, denominated or expressed in foreign currency, and includes securities expressed in foreign currency but where redemption or any form of return such as interest or dividends is payable in Indian currency - such a security STILL qualifies as a 'Foreign Security' under this inclusive limb, despite the Indian-currency payability of its return

Section 2(o) expressly extends 'Foreign Security' to cover securities expressed in foreign currency even where redemption or return (interest/dividends) is payable in Indian currency - the foreign-currency denomination, not the currency of the return, is what anchors the classification.

question_html: What is the 'first limb' of the section 2(v)(i) test for determining whether an individual is a 'Person Resident in India', and is citizenship relevant to this test?

options.A: The first limb requires residence in India for more than 182 days during the CURRENT financial year (not the preceding one), and citizenship is the decisive criterion for residential status
options.B: The first limb states that a person residing in India for more than 182 days during the course of the PRECEDING financial year will (at the threshold/basic level) be a Person Resident in India; citizenship is NOT the criterion for determining whether a person is resident in India - only the duration of stay in the preceding financial year matters at this threshold stage (subject to the exceptions in clauses (A) and (B))
options.C: The first limb has nothing to do with duration of stay at all and is determined purely by whether the individual holds an Indian passport
options.D: The first limb requires continuous, unbroken residence in India for the entire preceding financial year (365 days), with no threshold set at 182 days

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The first limb states that a person residing in India for more than 182 days during the course of the PRECEDING financial year will (at the threshold/basic level) be a Person Resident in India; citizenship is NOT the criterion for determining whether a person is resident in India - only the duration of stay in the preceding financial year matters at this threshold stage (subject to the exceptions in clauses (A) and (B))

The section 2(v)(i) first limb is a threshold test based on more than 182 days' residence in India during the PRECEDING financial year - not the current year - and citizenship plays no role in this determination, which is then subject to the clause (A)/(B) exceptions.

question_html: How does residential status under FEMA differ from residential status under the Income-tax Act, 1961, in terms of the point in time from which status is determined, and why does the study material say this distinction matters practically?

options.A: FEMA and the Income-tax Act, 1961 use an identical approach, determining residential status only for a complete financial year in both cases, with no distinction between the two
options.B: Under FEMA, residential status is determined for a complete calendar year (January to December), while under the Income-tax Act it is determined from a particular date
options.C: Under Income-tax law, a person's status is determined for a complete previous year, since tax liability arises with respect to the income of that previous year; under FEMA, being a regulatory law, residential status is NOT for a year but is determined FROM A PARTICULAR DATE - because one must know a person's status at the time of undertaking a transaction, and if status could only be known once a full year is completed, people would be unable to transact with that person in the interim
options.D: FEMA has no concept of residential status changing during a financial year at all - once a person's status is fixed at the start of a financial year, it remains fixed for the entire year regardless of subsequent events

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Under Income-tax law, a person's status is determined for a complete previous year, since tax liability arises with respect to the income of that previous year; under FEMA, being a regulatory law, residential status is NOT for a year but is determined FROM A PARTICULAR DATE - because one must know a person's status at the time of undertaking a transaction, and if status could only be known once a full year is completed, people would be unable to transact with that person in the interim

FEMA's date-based (rather than year-based) determination of residential status reflects its regulatory character - people transacting with an individual need to know that person's CURRENT status at the time of the transaction, not merely their status once an entire financial year has run its course.

options.A: A person who has gone out of India or who stays outside India will be a PROI (despite satisfying the 182-day test) if this is (a) for or on taking up employment outside India, or (b) for carrying on a business or vocation outside India, or (c) for any other purpose, in such circumstances as would indicate an intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period

options.A: Both are treated as a 'Person Resident in India' (PRII) - under clause (iii), an office, branch or agency in India owned or controlled by a PROI is itself a PRII (so that Indian residents can deal with such a branch in India without needing to treat it as a non-resident entity); under clause (iv), an office, branch or agency OUTSIDE India owned or controlled by a PRII is ALSO a PRII (so that a person cannot avoid FEMA by simply setting up a branch outside India)
options.B: An office, branch or agency in India owned by a PROI is treated as a PROI, while an office, branch or agency outside India owned by a PRII is treated as a PRII - the reverse of the correct rule
options.C: Both categories of office, branch or agency are treated as 'Persons Resident Outside India' regardless of who owns or controls them, since their physical location is irrelevant under FEMA
options.D: Neither an office, branch, nor agency can ever independently qualify as a 'person' or acquire any residential status of its own under FEMA - only the underlying owner's status is relevant

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Both are treated as a 'Person Resident in India' (PRII) - under clause (iii), an office, branch or agency in India owned or controlled by a PROI is itself a PRII (so that Indian residents can deal with such a branch in India without needing to treat it as a non-resident entity); under clause (iv), an office, branch or agency OUTSIDE India owned or controlled by a PRII is ALSO a PRII (so that a person cannot avoid FEMA by simply setting up a branch outside India)

Both clause (iii) (India-based office/branch/agency owned/controlled by a PROI) and clause (iv) (foreign-based office/branch/agency owned/controlled by a PRII) are deemed PRII - ensuring that Indian residents can freely deal with India-based branches of foreign entities, and that a PRII cannot sidestep FEMA merely by operating through a foreign branch.

question_html: Per the study material's example, an Indian resident imports machinery from a UK vendor for installation in a factory. Though 'machinery' is treated as 'capital expenditure' under accounting and income-tax law, why is this transaction nonetheless a CURRENT Account Transaction under FEMA?

options.A: The transaction is a Current Account Transaction under FEMA solely because the machinery is used for business purposes rather than personal consumption, a distinction FEMA treats as decisive regardless of asset/liability alteration
options.B: Under FEMA, once payment is made, the transaction does not alter (create) any asset in India for the UK vendor, nor does it create any liability to the UK vendor for the Indian importer - once payment is made, neither party owns or is owed anything in the other's country, so the transaction lacks the asset/liability-altering character that defines a 'Capital Account Transaction', making it a Current Account Transaction instead
options.C: The transaction is a Current Account Transaction under FEMA only because the amount involved is below a specific monetary threshold prescribed by the RBI for machinery imports
options.D: The classification under FEMA is identical to that under accounting and income-tax law, so this transaction is in fact treated as a Capital Account Transaction under FEMA as well

Correct answer: (B) Under FEMA, once payment is made, the transaction does not alter (create) any asset in India for the UK vendor, nor does it create any liability to the UK vendor for the Indian importer - once payment is made, neither party owns or is owed anything in the other's country, so the transaction lacks the asset/liability-altering character that defines a 'Capital Account Transaction', making it a Current Account Transaction instead

FEMA's capital-vs-current classification turns on whether a transaction alters cross-border assets/liabilities, not on accounting or tax treatment - a straightforward machinery import paid for in full, creating no ongoing asset or liability between the parties, is therefore a Current Account Transaction under FEMA despite being 'capital expenditure' for accounting purposes.

options.B: The gift remittance is treated as a Capital Account Transaction under FEMA (not a Current Account Transaction), consistent with its classification as a 'capital receipt' under accounts and income-tax law

question_html: What is the fundamental difference in legal consequence between a transaction listed in Schedule I versus one listed in Schedule II of the Current Account Transactions Rules, 2000?

options.A: There is no meaningful difference between Schedule I and Schedule II - both schedules list transactions that are equally and absolutely prohibited under all circumstances
options.B: A Schedule I transaction is absolutely PROHIBITED - foreign exchange cannot be drawn for it under any circumstances (unless the Rules themselves are amended); a Schedule II transaction, by contrast, is PERMITTED but only with the PRIOR APPROVAL of the specified Ministry/Department of the Government of India - the transaction is not banned outright, but conditional on obtaining that Governmental approval first
options.C: Schedule I transactions require RBI approval while Schedule II transactions are absolutely prohibited - the reverse of the correct distinction between the two schedules
options.D: Schedule I and Schedule II both list transactions that are freely permitted without any approval requirement, differing only in the specific Ministry responsible for record-keeping

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) A Schedule I transaction is absolutely PROHIBITED - foreign exchange cannot be drawn for it under any circumstances (unless the Rules themselves are amended); a Schedule II transaction, by contrast, is PERMITTED but only with the PRIOR APPROVAL of the specified Ministry/Department of the Government of India - the transaction is not banned outright, but conditional on obtaining that Governmental approval first

Schedule I bars drawal of foreign exchange outright for the listed purposes, while Schedule II permits it conditionally, subject to obtaining prior approval from the relevant Central Government Ministry/Department named against each transaction category.

question_html: Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), what is the overall annual limit for resident individuals (including minors), what special requirement applies for a minor remitter, and what is the general rule (with an exception) on consolidating remittances of family members?

options.A: Under the LRS, all resident individuals, including minors, are allowed to freely remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year (April-March) for any permissible current or capital account transaction (or a combination of both); if the remitter is a minor, the LRS declaration form must be countersigned by the minor's natural guardian; remittances under the Scheme CAN be consolidated for family members (subject to individual compliance), EXCEPT that clubbing is NOT permitted by other family members for capital account transactions (like opening a bank account, investment, or property purchase) unless those family members are co-owners/co-partners of the relevant overseas asset
options.B: The LRS excludes minors entirely, permitting only adult individuals to remit any amount, and family consolidation of remittances is never permitted under any circumstances whatsoever
options.C: The LRS overall limit is USD 250,000 per individual per LIFETIME (not per financial year), and no countersignature of any kind is required where the remitter is a minor
options.D: Family members can always consolidate remittances for capital account transactions such as property purchase, regardless of whether they are co-owners of the relevant asset

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Under the LRS, all resident individuals, including minors, are allowed to freely remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year (April-March) for any permissible current or capital account transaction (or a combination of both); if the remitter is a minor, the LRS declaration form must be countersigned by the minor's natural guardian; remittances under the Scheme CAN be consolidated for family members (subject to individual compliance), EXCEPT that clubbing is NOT permitted by other family members for capital account transactions (like opening a bank account, investment, or property purchase) unless those family members are co-owners/co-partners of the relevant overseas asset

The LRS sets a USD 250,000 per-financial-year limit applicable even to minors (whose declaration form needs a natural guardian's countersignature), and while family remittances can generally be consolidated, that consolidation is specifically barred for capital account transactions (like property/investment) where the other family members are not co-owners/co-partners.

question_html: Under Schedule III, what threshold triggers the requirement of prior RBI approval for donations by persons other than individuals (e.g., companies), and for what three categories of purposes does this threshold apply?

options.A: The threshold for such donations is a flat USD 10,000,000 regardless of the donor's foreign exchange earnings, with no reference to any percentage-of-earnings calculation
options.B: Prior RBI approval is required for donations exceeding 1% of the entity's foreign exchange earnings during the previous three financial years, OR USD 5,000,000, WHICHEVER IS LESS, for: (a) creation of Chairs in reputed educational institutes, (b) contribution to funds (not being an investment fund) promoted by educational institutes, and (c) contribution to a technical institution or body/association in the field of activity of the donor company
options.C: Approval is required for ANY donation of any amount whatsoever by a person other than an individual, with no monetary threshold at all under Schedule III
options.D: The threshold is 1% of foreign exchange earnings OR USD 5,000,000, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER (not lower), making larger, not smaller, donation amounts exempt from RBI approval

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Prior RBI approval is required for donations exceeding 1% of the entity's foreign exchange earnings during the previous three financial years, OR USD 5,000,000, WHICHEVER IS LESS, for: (a) creation of Chairs in reputed educational institutes, (b) contribution to funds (not being an investment fund) promoted by educational institutes, and (c) contribution to a technical institution or body/association in the field of activity of the donor company

Schedule III sets a 'lesser of' test for non-individual donations toward educational Chairs, educational-institute funds, or technical institutions/bodies related to the donor's field - approval is needed once the donation exceeds 1% of the entity's preceding-three-years' forex earnings or USD 5,000,000, whichever figure is LOWER.

Correct answer: (C) Prior RBI approval is required for remittances exceeding USD 10,000,000 per project for consultancy services in respect of INFRASTRUCTURE projects, and exceeding USD 1,000,000 per project for OTHER (non-infrastructure) consultancy services procured from outside India - so infrastructure consultancy carries a ten-times-higher approval-free threshold than other consultancy services

question_html: Under what circumstance is prior approval NOT required for a Schedule II or Schedule III transaction that would otherwise need it, in relation to (a) a Resident Foreign Currency (RFC) account, (b) an Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency (EEFC) account, and (c) payment via International Credit Card while abroad - subject to what exception for EEFC?

options.A: Approval is required for every RFC and EEFC account remittance without exception, and International Credit Card payments made abroad always require prior RBI approval regardless of purpose
options.B: The RFC/EEFC exemptions apply only to Schedule I (prohibited) transactions, converting otherwise-prohibited transactions into freely permitted ones once routed through an RFC or EEFC account
options.C: International Credit Card payments abroad are treated identically to cash withdrawals from an ordinary savings account, with no special exemption of any kind under the Current Account Transactions Rules
options.D: No approval is required where a Schedule II or Schedule III remittance is made from an RFC account, or from an EEFC account (subject to certain listed exceptions - such as P&I Club membership remittance, or the agent-commission/pre-incorporation-expense-reimbursement transactions - which still require approval even from an EEFC account); similarly, if a person on a visit abroad incurs Schedule III expenditure through an International Credit Card, no prior approval is required for that payment either

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No approval is required where a Schedule II or Schedule III remittance is made from an RFC account, or from an EEFC account (subject to certain listed exceptions - such as P&I Club membership remittance, or the agent-commission/pre-incorporation-expense-reimbursement transactions - which still require approval even from an EEFC account); similarly, if a person on a visit abroad incurs Schedule III expenditure through an International Credit Card, no prior approval is required for that payment either

Remittances for Schedule II/III purposes from RFC or EEFC accounts are generally exempt from the approval requirement (though certain specific EEFC remittances, like P&I Club membership or high-value agent commissions/pre-incorporation reimbursements, still need approval), and expenditure incurred abroad via International Credit Card for Schedule III purposes is similarly exempt from prior approval.

question_html: By virtue of the Finance Act, 2015 (made effective from 15th October, 2019), how were the powers to regulate capital account transactions split between the Reserve Bank of India and the Central Government?

options.A: Powers for regulation of Capital Account Transactions involving NON-DEBT instruments were transferred to the Central Government (which, in consultation with the RBI, may prescribe permissible classes of such transactions, admissible limits, and conditions under section 6(2A)); the RBI continued to have powers to regulate transactions involving DEBT instruments (specifying, in consultation with the Central Government, permissible classes of such transactions, admissible limits, and conditions under section 6(2)); for investment by Indian residents outside India, the RBI continues to have power to regulate transactions for both equity and debt
options.B: All powers to regulate capital account transactions, whether involving debt or non-debt instruments, were transferred entirely and exclusively to the Central Government, with the RBI retaining no role whatsoever
options.C: The RBI retained exclusive power over non-debt instruments while the Central Government took over exclusive power for debt instruments - the reverse of the actual 2019 split
options.D: The Finance Act, 2015 abolished the distinction between capital and current account transactions altogether, treating all foreign exchange transactions as a single unified category

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Powers for regulation of Capital Account Transactions involving NON-DEBT instruments were transferred to the Central Government (which, in consultation with the RBI, may prescribe permissible classes of such transactions, admissible limits, and conditions under section 6(2A)); the RBI continued to have powers to regulate transactions involving DEBT instruments (specifying, in consultation with the Central Government, permissible classes of such transactions, admissible limits, and conditions under section 6(2)); for investment by Indian residents outside India, the RBI continues to have power to regulate transactions for both equity and debt

The effective-15th-October-2019 split under the Finance Act, 2015 gives the Central Government power over non-debt-instrument capital account transactions (section 6(2A)) while the RBI retains power over debt-instrument capital account transactions (section 6(2)) - with RBI additionally retaining power over outbound (resident-to-abroad) equity and debt investment.

options.A: The proviso permits the RBI and Central Government to impose UNLIMITED restrictions specifically on amortisation of loans and depreciation of direct investments, singling these two categories out for heightened control
options.B: The proviso states that the Reserve Bank or the Central Government shall NOT impose any restrictions on the drawal of foreign exchange for payment due on account of (a) amortisation of loans, or (b) depreciation of direct investments, in the ordinary course of business - these two categories of drawal are protected from restriction under section 6

question_html: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Permissible Capital Account Transactions) Regulations, 2000, into what three categories is a capital account transaction basically split?

options.B: The three categories are 'current account', 'capital account', and 'miscellaneous account' transactions, a categorisation drawn from section 2 rather than the Permissible Capital Account Transactions Regulations, 2000

options.B: No - for medical treatment abroad (item (vii) of Schedule III), an individual may avail of foreign exchange facility for an amount in EXCESS of the USD 250,000 limit WITHOUT RBI approval, if it is so required by the medical institute offering the treatment; since Mr. Bhatt's USD 280,000 figure is based on the US hospital's own estimate, he does not require prior RBI approval for this amount
options.C: Yes - Mr. Bhatt must obtain prior RBI approval, but only for the USD 30,000 portion exceeding USD 250,000, while the first USD 250,000 can be drawn without any approval

Schedule III's proviso specifically exempts medical treatment abroad (among three specified purposes) from the USD 250,000 cap, permitting the full estimated amount from the treating medical institute to be drawn without RBI approval - so Mr. Bhatt's full USD 280,000 is covered without needing prior RBI approval.
